articles.title: Barefoot mom in sari runs 3km to win Rs 5k for kids' education
articles.summary: India News: PUNE: Ramabai Ranvir had no idea what running a race meant. All she had heard was there was Rs 3,000 to be won if she finished first.So, the 47-year-o.
articles.body: PUNE: Ramabai Ranvir had no idea what running a race meant. All she had heard was there was Rs 3,000 to be won if she finished first.So, the 47-year-old widow hopped onto the pickup with a group of police aspirants from the Beed academy where she worked, hoping to compete in what would be the first race of her life. It didn't bother her that she hadn't trained for the rigours of a long-distance run. It hardly mattered that she was the lone runner without shoes.In her sari, barefoot after her slippers gave up midway through the run, Ramabai ran 3km with the indomitable spirit of a mother competing for a cash prize that would ease her struggle to pay for her daughters' education, repo-rts Ardhra Nair."I ran like my life depended on it. I didn't know how much time I needed to cover the distance. I only sto-pped once I was past the finish line," she told TOI. "I am so happy they gave me Rs 5,000 instead of Rs 3,000. I bought notebooks and pens for my daughter Pooja. The remaining money is for Arti."Ramabai works in the kitchen at Dnyandeep Acad-emy, making over 200 chapatis a day for a monthly salary of Rs 9,000.The native of Potra, Hingoli, took the job to fund the education of her two daughters after her husband died in 2012.On Aug 28, her younger daughter Arti (20), a BSc computer science student who lives alone in Nanded, called asking for money for food and rent. Ramabai, who didn't have any cash to spare, had a sleepless night.At dawn, she heard the academy's trainers rounding up aspirants for a running competition nearby. She instantly decided to join in."There is no pain worse than that of not being able to take care of your children. The moment I came to know of the race, winning was the only thing on my mind."Datta Darade, who heads the academy, said Ramabai's determination moved him. The academy had enrolled her elder daughter Pooja (22) free of cost and given her employment and a room to stay in. "I was taking my students to the marathon. When Ramabai said she wanted to come along, I asked her, 'What will you do there?' She said, 'I will run.' I couldn't believe it when she won in the above-30 category."Pooja finished second in the 18-30 age group and won Rs 2,000. Arti said she was dumbstruck when her sister called to say their mother had won."Our mother studied till Class 7 and has worked all her life, not taking breaks even when she was unwell. She didn't hesitate to send me to Nanded for my studies. I am not surprised she decided to win a race for her family," she said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2001, scientists released 880 tiny weevils against a weed choking Texas waterways; by 2003, giant salvinia had almost disappeared
articles.summary: US News: A thick green carpet can make a pond or reservoir appear almost solid, but giant salvinia is a floating fern, spreading across the water rather than g.
articles.body: A thick green carpet can make a pond or reservoir appear almost solid, but giant salvinia is a floating fern, spreading across the water rather than growing from the bottom. In Texas and Louisiana, the plant had become difficult to manage, forming dense mats that blocked sunlight, reduced oxygen and interfered with waterways. According to the US Department of Agriculture, in 2001, researchers tried something considerably smaller. They released 880 salvinia weevils at four sites in eastern Texas and western Louisiana. Each adult was only about 2mm long, yet the insect was closely adapted to feeding on giant salvinia. The adults attacked growing tips while their larvae fed inside the plant.By September 2003, giant salvinia covered only about 1% of the water surface at the release sites, while untreated control areas remained completely covered. The experiment offered a striking example of biological control, using one small species to put pressure on another that had spread across large areas.In 2001, researchers turned to a tiny weevil to fight a giant aquatic weedThe salvinia weevil is native to parts of South America, including south-eastern Brazil, where it occurs alongside giant salvinia. It had already attracted attention as a biological control agent because its life cycle is closely tied to the plant.The US programme did not simply release insects at random. After host-range testing established that the Brazilian population was suitable for use against giant salvinia, permission was obtained for releases in eastern Texas and western Louisiana. The first successful US releases took place on 10 and 11 October 2001, when 880 adult weevils were placed at four sites.The insects were small enough to be easily overlooked. Adults are only about 2mm long, roughly the size of a kiwi seed, and can hide among dense vegetation. Their larvae are even harder to spot because much of their development takes place inside the plant.The giant salvinia problem grew from 124 acres to more than 3,000Giant salvinia, Salvinia molesta, is a floating fern rather than a conventional weed growing from the soil. Under favourable conditions, it can spread rapidly across the surface of ponds, canals and reservoirs.The resulting mats can become dense enough to shut out sunlight and reduce oxygen levels in the water. They also interfere with boating and can crowd out native vegetation. By the early 2000s, the plant had become a serious management problem in parts of Texas and Louisiana.At Toledo Bend Reservoir, the scale of the problem was already increasing sharply. As reported by the Texas State Government, giant salvinia covered about 124 acres in 2003, then expanded to more than 3,000 acres in 2004 despite continuing herbicide treatments.The contrast helps explain why biological control attracted interest. Spraying could suppress the plant, but giant salvinia kept growing and could occupy areas that were difficult for treatment boats to reach.How salvinia weevils slowly starve giant salvinia of nutrientsAdult weevils feed on the growing parts of salvinia, particularly nitrogen-rich buds. Females lay their eggs in small crevices around the plant's growing tips.Once the larvae hatch, they initially feed on the plant's outer tissues before moving into the rhizome. Their feeding interferes with the movement of nutrients towards new growth. As the damage accumulates, the plants weaken, turn brown and eventually die.That combination gives the insect two ways of slowing the fern. Adults reduce new growth from above, while larvae damage the plant internally.There is a timing element, too. At around 26°C, the journey from egg to adult takes roughly 45 days, and several generations can be produced during a suitable growing season.How tiny weevils brought giant salvinia under controlThe most useful evidence came from comparing sites where weevils had been released with nearby areas where they had not.By September 2003, giant salvinia covered only about 1% of the water surface at release sites. At the untreated control sites, it covered 100% of the surface. At some locations, biomass fell from more than 100 tons of fresh plant material per acre to less than two tons. Two sites, one in Texas and one in Louisiana, had gone from being almost completely covered to having mostly open water.The result was not simply a short-lived effect from releasing hungry insects. The weevils had survived and reproduced.That was important because an earlier attempt had not worked. Weevils released in Texas in 1999 had failed to establish after the experimental plots were affected by herbicide treatments, floods or drought. The later programme used weevils from the Brazilian population and produced a much more durable result.The 2001 weevil releases survived freezing Texas and Louisiana wintersGetting the weevils established was not guaranteed. In the winter following the 2001 releases, researchers returned to the Texas and Louisiana sites to see whether the insects had survived. Adults were found at two of the four release locations. The observations showed that Cyrtobagous salviniae could persist through temperatures that fell as low as −9.1°C at Toledo Bend and −7.1°C at Lake Texana.Cold remains a limitation for the insect, though. Attempts to establish populations farther north have been unsuccessful in some areas, probably because freezing winter temperatures kill the weevils. Researchers have therefore continued looking at cold-tolerant populations and ways of improving winter survival.So the insect was not a universal solution. Its effectiveness depended partly on whether the local climate allowed it to persist.Weevil feeding turns giant salvinia brown before the dead mats sinkAs feeding weakens a dense stand of giant salvinia, the vegetation turns brown and begins to collapse. Once the floating mat dies, it sinks as it decomposes, allowing sunlight to penetrate the water again. The nutrients held in the plant material are returned to the water column rather than remaining locked in the floating vegetation.The weevils themselves do not need to be manually moved from plant to plant. Adults can walk across dense mats, fly at night and move with floating vegetation or floodwaters. Water managers can also introduce mass-reared insects into newly affected areas.From Australia to the US, the salvinia weevil spread as a natural controlThe US experience became part of a wider history of using the salvinia weevil against giant salvinia. Before the Texas and Louisiana programme, the insect had already been used successfully in Australia and subsequently released in a number of other countries.The early Texas and Louisiana results nevertheless provided a clear demonstration of what could happen when the right insect established itself alongside the invasive plant.A weed that had been covering entire stretches of water was being eaten by a beetle small enough to fit on a fingertip. By 2003, at the monitored release sites, the difference was already measurable: about 1% cover where the weevils had been introduced compared with complete surface cover at the untreated controls.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Conservative journalists fire back at Washington Post after report claiming Pentagon 'secretly installed' them
articles.summary: Rob Maness, Kurt Schlichter and Thomas Anderson fired back at The Washington Post over a report on Sunday suggesting they were "installed" by the Pentagon.
articles.body: Conservative journalists attacked The Washington Post for a report on Sunday suggesting they were "secretly installed" by the Pentagon to push pro-Trump administration narratives. The article, written by Dan Lamothe and Tara Copp, suggested that former military members Rob Maness, Kurt Schlichter and Thomas Anderson were hired as "civilian employees" under the Pentagon, adding that each has supported Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and attacked critics of the Trump administration's military strategy. "The Pentagon has secretly installed several conservative military veterans with large online followings in government roles, declining to disclose their assignments as they amplify Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's viewpoints and attack those who scrutinize the Trump administration, according to people familiar with the matter and corroborating material," the report read. It continued, "At least some of the influencers have been assigned to civilian roles that could lead to changes in policy, the people familiar with the matter said." HEGSETH ANNOUNCES JOINT TASK FORCE WITH DOJ TO PROSECUTE LEAKS TO JOURNALISTS 'WITH THE FULL FORCE OF THE LAW' After the article was published, Maness, Schlichter and Anderson pushed back on its implications, accusing the publication of using illegally obtained information to frame them as federal plants. Each clarified that they were invited by the Department of War to take part as advisors in a task force studying senior service colleges through their military experience and past commentary on ways to improve the institutions. They added that they were previously compensated only for their roles in the task force, which has since concluded. "My service with the Department of War as a 'Special Government Employee' was exclusively limited to participation in such task force and ended on July 26, 2026," Anderson, under the account "Cynical Publius," posted to X Sunday. "At no time have I ever received any compensation of any kind from any government source of any kind for anything I write or have ever written on X or in any magazine or other source. Those who claim otherwise defame me. I proudly and unabashedly support the efforts of President Trump and the Department of War because it’s the right thing to do." FIRED STARS AND STRIPES STAFFERS SUE PENTAGON, ALLEGE RETALIATION AND FIRST AMENDMENT VIOLATION Maness wrote on X Monday, "The Washington Post article published about me attempts to establish a context with its subtitle that is completely fabricated, categorically false, and defames me. The article also publishes illegally obtained personally identifiable information from government data sources about me. I patriotically and unashamedly support the efforts of President Trump, Secretary Hegseth, and the Department of War to ensure we are producing senior officers who can win our nation’s wars because it’s the most impactful thing to do for America’s future." Schlichter published his own article critiquing The Washington Post in his column on Townhall.com on Monday. "The leftists who seized on this innuendo don’t care about the truth, and it’s irrelevant whether the regime media reporters wrote garbage on purpose or because they are grossly incompetent. I don’t argue with people who, through malice or ineptitude, act in bad faith unless I’m in court. But I will use this situation as a cautionary example of why the regime media is trash and why your contempt for it is so well-deserved," Schlichter wrote, adding that the original piece misspelled his name. HEGSETH EXCORIATES MEDIA, LIKENING THEM TO ‘PHARISEES’ IN TRUMP DEFENSE In a comment to Fox News Digital, Post journalist Dan Lamothe said the article was "accurate as written" in that neither the journalists nor the Pentagon "disclosed they were special government employees" while they were commenting on Pentagon matters. The Washington Post did not immediately respond to a request for additional comment. When reached for a comment, the Pentagon pointed to a comment written by Under Secretary of War Anthony Tata on X Sunday. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Senior officers deserve the best possible education: effective, unbiased & laser-focused on our core warfighting mission. @SecWar directed a Senior Service College Task Force to conduct a comprehensive review of @DeptofWar SSCs. Its mandate: ensure these institutions are anchored in military history, strategy, high standards, meritocracy & overall excellence. That review is now complete. Special thanks to @RobManess, @KurtSchlichter & Tom Anderson for answering the call to serve on this Task Force. Led by Dr. Maurice L. Todd—ASW(R), PhD, MA, MS & top 5% West Point graduate—they delivered critical recommendations to strengthen our SSCs & prepare our military leaders to achieve peace through strength," Tata wrote.

articles.title: Like 23 Silkyaras at once, says Aus expert on Nepal's rescue challenge
articles.summary: South Asia News: TRISHULI BAZAAR/DEHRADUN: Australian tunnelling expert Arnold Dix, who became widely known in India for his role in the 2023 Silkyara (Uttarakhand) tu.
articles.body: TRISHULI BAZAAR/DEHRADUN: Australian tunnelling expert Arnold Dix, who became widely known in India for his role in the 2023 Silkyara (Uttarakhand) tunnel rescue, has described the search operation around Nepal's flood-ravaged hydropower projects as being like "23 Silkyaras going on at the same time".Dix, advising Nepal govt on rescue efforts at Trishuli 3A hydropower project, told TOI Tuesday that the disaster was unlike a conventional tunnel rescue. He said 27 hydropower plants were damaged, with 12 suffering severe damage. He is overseeing the Trishuli 3A operation, where around 50 lives could be at stake.At the project, teams are working to drain water from an access tunnel and clear the route towards the powerhouse, where survivors may be trapped. "We've had some good progress today," Dix said. "We're now at that critical stage where we've found the tunnel, we're getting water out, and we can start to head up towards the power station."However, he warned rescuers may have to dig 10m or 100m depending on how much mud and water filled the tunnel. Breaking through a blockage could release trapped water if the emergency shutdown failed. Large boulders could also slow excavation.Dix said he was fortunate to be working with "a team of fantastic Indian Army engineers" who had also worked with him during Silkyara rescue. Draining the tunnel could also lower water levels inside the powerhouse, he said.Once water is drained and access established, rescuers will excavate towards the powerhouse, which Dix compared to Silkyara, when 41 workers were brought out alive after being trapped for 17 days.Asked whether teams received signs of survivors, Dix said absence of signals could not be treated as proof that nobody was alive. He remained hopeful that if workers had survived, they were likely to be in upper part of the powerhouse.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Hikers heard ‘howling’ from a California water tank; rescuers found a mother bear and her cubs trapped inside and spent hours freeing them
articles.summary: US News: On a late-August afternoon in the San Gabriel Mountains, a group of hikers near La Verne, California, heard an unsettling sound: what they described a.
articles.body: On a late-August afternoon in the San Gabriel Mountains, a group of hikers near La Verne, California, heard an unsettling sound: what they described as “howling” coming from a large water tank along a trail. When they investigated, they discovered a mother black bear and her two cubs trapped inside the cistern, unable to climb out. Wildlife officials and fire crews responded, spending hours delicately extracting the bears and reuniting them before releasing the family back into the wild. The dramatic rescue, reported by local news outlets, underscores the dangers that human infrastructure can pose to wildlife in Southern California’s bear country.A strange sound on the trailThe incident began on August 28, 2026, in the hills above La Verne, a city at the base of the San Gabriel Mountains about 35 miles east of downtown Los Angeles. Hikers on a popular trail near a water cistern reported hearing unusual vocalisations, described in some accounts as howling or crying—coming from the structure.Curious and concerned, they approached the tank and peered inside. What they saw was a mother black bear and two small cubs, pacing and calling from within the steep-sided container. The bears had apparently climbed in to reach water but found the smooth, vertical walls impossible to scale on the way out.Wildlife officials and fire crews respondThe hikers alerted authorities, and a multi-agency response quickly formed. That’s when the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW), local fire departments and wildlife experts showed up to evaluate the situation and devise a rescue plan. Water cisterns like this are common in remote hiking areas, where they act as water reservoirs for firefighting or trail maintenance. But for wildlife, these cisterns can become deadly traps. Animals can climb in but often struggle to climb out, especially if the walls are slick and without footholds. Bears, with their strong climbing ability and curious nature, are particularly vulnerable. Rescuers knew they had to be careful. A stressed mother bear with cubs is dangerous and a wrong move could injure the animals or put people in danger.Hours of careful work to free the bearsThe rescue operation took several hours. Crews first had to secure the area and keep onlookers at a safe distance. Then, with the help of specialised equipment and techniques, they worked to get the bears out one by one. Reports describe rescuers lowering harnesses or ropes into the cistern and gently fastening the cubs before pulling them out. The mother bear required more time and care. Wildlife officials sedated the animal in some versions to take care of her safely, while others describe a more “hands-on” extraction with minimal drugs to avoid unnecessary risk. The goal was the same either way: get all three bears out alive and in good condition. Once the cubs had been removed, they were kept nearby so the family could be reunited as soon as the mother was freed. Reunited and released Once the mother bear was finally extracted, rescuers checked the family for injuries and allowed them to recover briefly. Fortunately, all three appeared to be in decent condition despite the ordeal.CDFW and partner agencies then transported the bears to a suitable location within their home range and released them back into the wild. The exact release site was not disclosed, as is standard practice to avoid drawing people to the animals or encouraging habituation.In statements after the rescue, officials emphasised that the outcome could have been very different without the hikers’ quick reporting and the coordinated response.Why water tanks are a hidden dangerIncidents like this are more common than many people realise. Across California and other Western states, open or poorly secured water tanks, cisterns and stock ponds have trapped and killed bears, deer, mountain lions and other wildlife. Animals are drawn to these sources, especially during hot, dry months when natural water can be scarce.Once inside, smooth concrete or metal walls offer no grip, and the depth can be too great for animals to jump or climb out. Over time, many animals die from exhaustion, injury or dehydration.Wildlife agencies and land managers have been working to reduce these risks by installing wildlife escape ramps or ladders in tanks and ponds; fencing off or covering cisterns in high-use areas; and retrofitting older structures with bear-proof designs. But thousands of tanks remain, especially on remote public and private lands, making them an ongoing hazard.What hikers and residents can doThe La Verne rescue underscores the role that the public plays in wildlife safety. Hikers, runners and residents who spend time in bear country can help by:Reporting trapped or injured wildlife immediately to CDFW, local sheriff’s departments or fire agencies; keeping a safe distance and not attempting to feed or handle wild animals; noting landmarks or GPS coordinates to help responders find the location quickly.In this case, the hikers’ decision to investigate the “howling” and then call for help made the difference between a tragic story and a successful rescue.Bears in the San Gabriel MountainsBlack bears are native to the San Gabriel Mountains and have become increasingly visible as human development expands into their habitat. They play an important ecological role, dispersing seeds, scavenging carrion and helping regulate populations of smaller animals.At the same time, bears that become habituated to human food or garbage can end up in conflict with people, sometimes with fatal results for the bears. That’s why agencies emphasise secure trash, proper food storage and avoiding intentional feeding.Rescues like the La Verne cistern incident show another side of the human–bear relationship: when infrastructure unintentionally endangers wildlife, and people step in to correct the problem.A reminder to secure our footprintFor wildlife managers, the incident is a reminder to keep auditing and retrofitting water infrastructure in bear country. For residents and visitors, it’s a reminder that even well-meaning structures, like a water tank meant to support trails or firefighting, can have unintended consequences for the animals that share the landscape.The mother bear and her cubs are now back in the forest, free to forage, den and raise their young without the threat of a concrete trap. And the hikers who heard their calls will have a story to tell for years: the day they followed a strange sound and helped bring a bear family home.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Odisha: Why Dara Singh, murderer of Christian missionary Graham Staines and his sons, may walk free in India
articles.summary: Dara Singh is serving a life sentence for burning alive Graham Staines and his two sons in Odisha in 1999.
articles.body:
One of India's most shocking incidents of anti-Christian violence is back in the news more than a quarter of a century after it drew condemnation from around the world.

On Wednesday, the Supreme Court is due to take a call on a petition seeking release from prison by a man, who is convicted of killing Australian Christian missionary Graham Staines and his two young sons in 1999.

Dara Singh - whose real name is Rabindra Kumar Pal - has been in jail since his arrest in 2000, serving a life sentence for burning alive the Australian missionary and his six and 10-year-old sons in a village in the eastern state of Odisha (formerly Orissa).

Staines had spent 30 years working with leprosy patients, but Singh and his associates from Hindu hardline groups had accused him of forcibly converting poor Hindus from disadvantaged castes and tribals to Christianity.

The viciousness of the crime sent shockwaves through India's minority Christian community and caused global outrage. Now reports that Singh may be set free have brought alive memories of the heinous crime.

Staines lived in Baripada in Mayurbhanj district, where he worked among the local tribal community.

On the night of their murder on 22 January 1999, Staines and his sons had attended a Christian gathering in Manoharpur, a remote village in the neighbouring district of Keonjhar. They were sleeping in their jeep when a mob of 60 to 70 people led by Singh surrounded their vehicle, set fire to it and prevented them from escaping.

As Singh went on the run after the crime, police put up posters all over the state, offering an 800,000-rupee (approximately $18,000 then) reward for information leading to his capture. Reports at the time said he was helped by villagers and tribals who eulogised him as "a modern-day Tarzan who plays with elephants and rides tigers". He was arrested a year later during an overnight raid on a jungle hideout.

In a sensational interview with the India Today magazine's Ruben Banerjee from prison a few months later, he denied killing Staines and his children but said he "did not like Graham Staines" and had "spearheaded the movement against missionaries".

"Missionaries have been targeting our religion. They have been converting Hindus by deceit and inducements. Our religion is under siege. As a true Hindu, it was my responsibility to oppose them," he said. "Since I was possibly the most famous name in the region, the police implicated me in the killings."

Singh added that he was "prepared to be a martyr for the cause of Hindus" but believed that he would never get convicted.

His optimism was misplaced - in 2003, a trial court sentenced Singh to death and 12 others to life imprisonment. Two years later, the high court commuted his death sentence. It confirmed the life term of his accomplice Mahendra Hembram but freed 11 others, saying there was not enough evidence to support their convictions.

In January 2011, the Supreme Court upheld Singh's life sentence, refusing the prosecutors' plea to reinstate the death penalty.

The Staines murder was not the only crime Singh was guilty of. In 2007, he was convicted for two other heinous crimes he committed against religious minorities in 1999 - the same year he murdered the Australian missionary and his children.

He received life sentences for leading a mob that set fire to a church and killed Catholic priest Arul Das with an arrow as he tried to flee the burning building and, in the second instance, for beating and burning to death a Muslim garment trader Shaikh Rahaman.

Police had registered 10 cases accusing Singh of involvement in hijacking trucks of Muslim traders transporting cows - an animal many Hindus consider sacred - and setting them free. In his interview, Singh denied being "involved personally", saying "my supporters might have done it". But he admitted that he was "actively involved in the movement against illegal trade in cows and cowslaughter" which "had to be stopped at any cost".

Church leaders had alleged the attacks were carried out at the behest of hardline Hindu organisation Bajrang Dal but Singh denied he was a member and an enquiry commission, led by retired top court judge DP Wadhwa, later ruled that he had worked alone.

Graham Staines' widow, Gladys, who stayed on in India with her daughter Esther until July 2004, said she had "forgiven" Dara Singh in the Christian spirit. "Forgiveness opens up the path of healing," she said.

In July 2024, Singh filed a plea for remission in the top court, saying he was entitled to be released because he had spent more than 25 years in prison. He said his conduct had been good in jail and expressed remorse for his actions.

The 62-year-old blamed the crime on "the fervour of youth" in his petition seeking early release.

"The petitioner acknowledges and deeply regrets the transgressions committed more than two decades ago.

"In the fervour of youth, fuelled by impassioned reactions to the brutal history of India, the petitioner's psyche momentarily lost restraint and it is imperative for the court to scrutinise not merely the actions but the underlying intent, noting that there was no personal animosity harboured towards any victim," he wrote.

Last year, the top court asked the state government to take a call on his plea, but the authorities have so far not told the court what they intend to do.

At the last hearing on 19 August, authorities told the court that the Sentence Review Board (SRB), which is examining Singh's plea, was waiting for some more paperwork and sought an adjournment.

The two-judge bench of Justices Manoj Misra and Vijay Bishnoi expressed their annoyance at the several adjournments the state had sought in the case and said if the SRB failed to decide Singh's plea by 2 September, the court would. "You take a decision, whichever way you want. If you do not take a decision, then we will."

Reports that Singh may walk free if the state government or the court accept his remission petition have led to some disquiet in India's 30-million Christian community - some of it because of unease over his earlier statements.

In his 2000 India Today interview, he said he had "no regrets" and "will never regret" killing Staines' children. "When Hindus die, others don't cry. Why should we weep when others die? Whatever has happened is right. Whatever will happen will also be right."

If released from prison, he said, he would "go back to what I have been doing - oppose cow slaughter and conversions".

"The government must stop them. If they are not stopped, more people might get killed. Anything can happen," he added.

In an article on the Union of Catholic News (UCN) website, human rights and Christian political activist John Dayal wrote recently that remission after decades in jail is "not unusual" in India and "the principle behind it - that punishment should allow for reform and eventual return to society - is humane".

But the anxiety among religious minorities in Odisha "is not abstract given the state's history of anti-Christian violence", Dayal points out, citing the Kandhamal riots of 2008 , in which dozens were killed and tens of thousands were displaced.

"The Staines murders were not an ordinary homicide but a public, theatrical act of terror, intended to be seen and understood as a warning. The killings of Father Arul Doss and Sheikh Rehman extended that same message," he writes.

"What remains to be seen is not whether Singh will eventually walk free, but how the government conducts itself around that decision...and whether minority communities are given any reassurance," Dayal adds.

articles.title: Duane Davis lawyer plans to appeal Tupac Shakur murder conviction
articles.summary: A day after Davis was found guilty of first-degree murder, his attorney told NBC News the defense had been preparing for an appeal before the trial even began.
articles.body: A day after a Las Vegas jury found Duane “Keffe D” Davis guilty of first-degree murder in the 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur, his attorney said the defense is looking toward its next fight, an appeal. Davis, 63, was convicted Monday of first-degree murder with use of a deadly weapon in the fatal drive-by shooting of Shakur nearly 30 years ago. His sentencing is Oct. 13, when he faces the possibility of spending the rest of his life in prison. “We were preparing for the appeal, so even Mr. Davis knew that going in,” defense attorney Michael Sanft told NBC News on Tuesday. “Even before the first set of jurors came in for jury selection, we knew it was going to be an appeal issue.” At the center of the appeal, Sanft said, will be the judge’s decision to allow jurors to hear statements Davis made to investigators under a 2008 proffer agreement. The agreement allowed him to speak candidly about what he did or witnessed that night in 1996 without facing charges. The defense unsuccessfully sought to exclude the proffer statements before trial, because, Sanft said, “we believed it was highly prejudicial.” Davis entered into the proffer agreement with federal investigators in 2008 as authorities investigated the killing of Christopher Wallace, the rapper known as the Notorious B.I.G. During those conversations, Davis provided investigators with information about Shakur’s killing. Prosecutors in the case of Shakur’s killing, however, ultimately used Davis’ own words as a central part of their case against him, playing recordings of his statements to investigators and pointing jurors to accounts he later gave in interviews and his 2019 memoir, “Compton Street Legend.” Sanft argued at trial that Davis had fabricated or embellished his accounts for money and notoriety and that investigators lacked physical evidence independently placing him at the scene of Shakur’s shooting. Davis did not testify in his own defense, but jurors heard extensively from him through those earlier recordings and public statements. Prosecutors called 24 witnesses in the 10-day trial. The defense called three witnesses. Prosecutors portrayed Davis as a “shotcaller” in the South Side Compton Crips in California who helped orchestrate the attack on Shakur after Shakur and others beat Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, Davis’ nephew, inside the MGM Grand earlier that night. Davis was not accused of firing the shots that killed Shakur. Prosecutors argued that he provided the gun and helped set the killing in motion. Under Nevada law, a person who aids or abets a murder can be held criminally responsible for the killing. On Sept. 7, 1996, Shakur was riding in a BMW driven by Death Row Records co-founder Marion “Suge” Knight near the Las Vegas Strip when a white Cadillac pulled alongside them and someone inside opened fire. Shakur, 25, was shot multiple times and died six days later. Knight survived. For decades, no one was charged in the killing. Davis became the only person ever prosecuted in connection with Shakur’s death after his public comments about the shooting helped revive investigators’ interest in the cold case. He is also the only person still alive who was believed to have been in the Cadillac when the shooting occurred. Sanft, however, said the defense continues to maintain that Davis was not in the car or in Las Vegas that night. The jury rejected that defense, returning a unanimous guilty verdict after less than three hours of deliberations. Sanft said the speed of the decision surprised him. “For a jury to come back 2½ hours after submitting it to them ... they had pretty much made up their minds,” he said. “We thought for sure they were going to, you know, spend time over the night to come back in the morning and really get into the evidence.” Sanft said Davis had been prepared for the possibility of a conviction because of the pretrial rulings. “There was an understanding that there’s a long game being played here,” Sanft said. “That this was not the end of the movie, but rather just a phase.” Sanft said the defense will seek the minimum possible sentence at Davis’ Oct. 13 sentencing, but he acknowledged that Davis could effectively spend the rest of his life behind bars. “Mr. Davis is in his 60s. He’s in his mid-60s,” Sanft said. “You know, at this particular point, any sentence is potentially going to be a life sentence for him. So, of course, we’ll be asking for the minimum, but that’s not a good option right now for him.” Despite the guilty verdict, Sanft said, Davis remains focused on what comes next. “No one ever wants to lose, especially something like this,” he said. “But ultimately, at the end of the day, he understands that this is the next step. We have to take it before an appellate court. We have to go through that process, and then we come back at some point.”

articles.title: Airline Defends Aerial Stunt After 2 of Its Planes Flew 50 Feet Above Stadium Packed with 50,000 Fans
articles.summary: South Africa’s Airlink confirmed civil aviation authorities approved the Cape Town rugby match stunt, which was flown by veteran pilots
articles.body:
Two passenger jets flew less than 50 feet above a packed stadium in South Africa over the weekend

Airlink, which operates the aircraft, defended the maneuver and cited careful planning, rehearsals and approval from aviation authorities

A similar flyover gained attention during the 1995 rugby World Cup in South Africa and was featured in the film Invictus

An airline is doubling down on its decision to fly two commercial jets less than 50 feet above a stadium packed with thousands of fans.

On Saturday, Aug. 29, two Embraer aircraft from South Africa-based carrier Airlink completed a low flyover at 55,000-seat DHL Stadium in Cape Town ahead of a rugby Test match between South Africa and New Zealand.

Footage of the aerial stunt quickly went viral on social media , with many praising the display from Airlink. The airline is the official sponsor of "Rugby's Greatest Rivalry," a four-match Test series between the two countries.

FlightRadar24 , an online flight tracker that uses real-time aviation data, later revealed that the "lead aircraft passed less than 50 feet above the top of the stadium." While some considered it to be a reckless maneuver, the airline defended the flyover online.

"Planning. Precision. Performance," Airlink wrote in the caption of a Facebook post alongside photos of the stunt on Saturday. "Spectacular scenes of Airlink's double Embraer flyover at the DHL Stadium."

In a statement shared with a local government news website , Airlink defended its actions further, saying, "The flight demanded careful planning and rehearsal, as it required navigating at low altitude," Airlink said. "The South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby."

The carrier noted that both aircraft were flown by highly experienced crews, each with its own commander, co-pilot and safety or technical officer.

"It's a well known fact that we have the best pilots in the world, that was spectacular," South Africa's Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie wrote in a Sunday, Aug. 30, X post.

This isn't the first time a stadium flyover in South Africa has captured international attention. Before the start of the 1995 rugby World Cup, a South African Airways jet flew over a Johannesburg stadium carrying the message "Good luck Bokke," a nod to South Africa's national rugby team, the Springboks.

articles.title: Rosie O’Donnell rants that Trump-era ICE facilities are concentration camps where inmates are raped
articles.summary: Rosie O'Donnell compared ICE detention facilities to concentration camps in Nazi Germany and suggested Dolly Parton should run the world instead.
articles.body: Actress Rosie O’Donnell compared ICE facilities to concentration camps in Nazi Germany in a video she posted on TikTok Friday. In a TikTok titled, "Friday Ramble," O'Donnell discussed a variety of topics, including the recent death of country music legend Dolly Parton, before launching into criticism of the Trump administration. "We all vowed ‘Never Again,’ remember?" she said in the TikTok video, referencing the Holocaust. She noted that people even today are shocked at how Germans allowed fascism to take over before claiming fascism is in full swing in the United States. "We’re making concentration camps. … We’re rounding up people without a warrant. We’re raping children in detention, in ICE detention. They’re all getting pregnant," she said. articles.title: Autonomous aircraft: Pilot-free crop dusters lead the way
articles.summary: Autonomous crop-spraying aircraft are leading the way in pilot-free flying.
articles.body:
Over an alfalfa field in California's San Joaquin Valley, a small crop-spraying plane is flying scarily low to the ground. There's little risk to humans though, as the plane is pilot-free.

"We can actually go lower than a human pilot can," says Russ Marotzke, as the aircraft skims over the crop.

Flying lower means less spray drift and therefore less chemicals are needed than in conventional manned crop-dusting, he says.

The pilotless plane belongs to Pyka, where Marotzke works as a flight test engineer.

Based in a converted Second World War hangar overlooking San Francisco Bay, the start-up makes self-flying aircraft without cockpits, designed either to spray crops or deliver cargo.

It is among a small group of companies racing to bring autonomous fixed-wing aircraft into commercial service.

Flying urban air taxis, so called electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft, have captured much of the attention around autonomous aviation.

But a quieter race is also under way to deploy self-flying planes, first for jobs like crop spraying and cargo delivery – and eventually, many of their makers hope, carrying passengers too.

"A fully scaled, ubiquitous passenger operation is the holy grail," says Michael Norcia, Pyka's co-founder and CEO, who envisions a large fleet of minibus-capacity Pyka planes ferrying passengers up and down the US east and west coasts.

"There's a decent chance we'll get to that point before the eVTOL industry."

I've come to one of Pyka's crop-sprayer test sites, about 80km (50 miles) east of the company's factory and reached by a bumpy dirt road.

Today, Marotzke and a colleague are trying out a software update on a demonstration aircraft.

About a dozen Pyka aircraft are already in Brazil where they are used to spray crops such as cotton and soybeans, work previously carried out by human pilots.

The crop-spraying plane is fully electric, with its battery in the nose. It can fly for about 35 minutes and carries up to 300L of spray in a tank in its middle.

Pyka's planes are sometimes called large drones, but it seems an understatement: they all have 11.5m wingspans.

Inside a shipping container beside the field, the engineers highlight on a computer the area they want the aircraft to spray. The software then plans the route, taking account of obstacles such as nearby power lines that have already been mapped.

The take-off, down a runway beside the field, is seamless. About 15 minutes later, after sensing that it is running low on spray – water for today's purposes – the aircraft lands itself for a manual refill and demonstration battery swap. It then takes to the air again to resume spraying precisely where it left off.

Autonomous flight is different from autopilot.

Autopilot assists, much like cruise control and lane-keeping functions in a car.

Autonomous systems aim to handle the entire flight, including take-off and landing, with little or no human intervention, using algorithms to process sensor data and control the aircraft.

Self-flying planes have been slower to emerge than self-driving cars, despite operating in what is generally considered a more structured and predictable environment.

That is partly because big tech companies "doubled down" on cars, pouring vast sums into the technology, says Mykel Kochenderfer, an expert in safe aviation autonomy at Stanford University.

But it is also because aircraft are held to stricter safety standards than cars, creating a much higher bar for deployment.

"The consequences for air accidents can just be so severe," says Kochenderfer.

Military interest has been helping propel the technology. Many of the companies have defence contracts to demonstrate and trial their systems, often with fewer regulatory hurdles than on the civilian side, and some are even already supplying military customers .

In the US, the largest autonomous fixed-wing aircraft approved for commercial civilian use so far is Pyka's crop sprayer, which won authorization last year.

Though operations are limited to a tightly defined agricultural setting and require a ground operator and visual observer. It earlier secured similar approval in Brazil, where rules are more permissive.

Pyka aims to scale up production from around two dozen planes a year currently to 1000 by 2030. Each sells for $550,000, with customers trained to operate them.

The UK has yet to approve any such longer-term operations, though British firm Windracers is seeking permission to launch an autonomous cargo service in Shetland and Orkney. Its aircraft, designed to carry goods to remote areas, are also flying missions in Ukraine.

"It would be the first heavy-lift air cargo service by drone certainly in the UK and probably anywhere," says Stephen Wright, Windracers founder and chairman.

Supporters say autonomous aircraft could address pilot shortages, remove people from dangerous work such as crop spraying, improve efficiency – for example, by allowing aircraft to carry more cargo – and cut costs if one operator can oversee many planes.

They also argue automation could make flying safer, pointing to past declines in accidents as more automated systems have been introduced.

The US Air Line Pilots Association (ALPA) calls removing pilots "a serious gamble with safety and a step too far".

The US National Agricultural Aviation Association, which represents crop dusting pilots, says small uncrewed aircraft can be hard for its aviators to see. Piloted planes, it adds, can spray a much larger area faster.

Pyka and Windracers are building aircraft from scratch, arguing this allows autonomy to be designed in from the outset and the aircraft tailored to the job.

Others are retrofitting existing larger planes.

Backed by Boeing's investment arm, US-based Reliable Robotics is currently testing its system on the Cessna 208B Grand Caravan, a single-pilot cargo plane that can carry about 1360kg of payload over hundreds of kilometers.

Retrofitting on certified aircraft lets the company focus exclusively on proving the autonomous system's safety rather than also having to seek approval for a new aircraft, says Robert Rose, its co-founder and CEO.

Merlin Labs, also US-based, has been working its way up through progressively larger military aircraft and is now applying its system to the two-pilot Lockheed Martin C-130J military transport plane, with commercial multi-crew cargo planes next.

"It is a common autonomy brain that can transition between different aircraft," explains Matt George, Merlin's founder and CEO.

The companies also differ in their approach to AI.

Reliable is avoiding it altogether, arguing it would complicate certification.

Merlin, meanwhile, is taking a far more AI-centric approach.

The divide is evident in so-called detect and avoid systems.

One of autonomous flight's biggest challenges is replicating a pilot's ability to spot and maneuver safely around other aircraft and obstacles, and there is virtually no margin for error.

With no perfect solution yet, companies are adding different sensor systems as well as duplicating those that already come as standard to provide extra back-up.

Reliable has added forward-looking air-to-air radar to detect other aircraft more than eight kilometers ahead, with software that follows fixed rules to decide how the plane should respond.

It is "better than a pilot's eyeballs" says Rose.

Merlin, meanwhile, is using AI-powered cameras to detect and classify objects.

Pyka has used lidar from the outset to detect trees, vehicles, large birds and terrain. But it's short range, so the company also plans to add AI-powered cameras, its first real use of AI onboard.

"For a lot of things there's no need to use AI…but for figuring out that six pixels in the distance are an airplane versus some other smudge, it is perfect territory," says Norcia.

The AI dilemma also extends to communicating with air traffic control.

In shared airspace, aircraft must be able to receive, interpret and respond to radio instructions, typically from air traffic control.

Reliable's solution is to have a remote pilot on the ground, initially fully trained, to handle communications and make safety-critical decisions.

Merlin plans to use generative AI, trained on thousands of hours of recorded exchanges, to interpret instructions and respond itself.

"Our problem is harder… but we want to move beyond remote piloting," says George.

Merlin plans to reduce pilots in stages, from two to one and eventually none.

Pyka, says Norcia, is content to let others "blaze the trail" in finding the best way to operate in shared airspace.

Meanwhile, even if fully autonomous passenger flight remains elusive, many expect the technology being pioneered will inch into commercial aviation, potentially making piloted flying safer.

That, notes ALPA, the US pilots' association, would be a welcome development.

articles.title: Rising numbers of children in mental health crisis ending up in A&E
articles.summary: NHS emergency departments are seeing more cases of self-harm, eating disorders and emotional distress in young people.
articles.body:
There has been a sharp rise in children and young people attending A&E units in England in a mental health crisis, NHS doctors are warning.

The number of six to 17-year-olds turning up in significant distress for things like self-harm and eating disorders, or in emotional crisis, rose by 36% between 2019 and 2025, according to the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health analysis.

Some faced waits of more than 12 hours once there. The college said A&Es were not the best place for them, but a lack of support in the community meant they often had nowhere else to turn.

The government said it was looking to improve services and would be setting out plans soon.

The analysis – based on figures provided under the Freedom of Information Act by NHS England – found there were 75,491 attendances at A&E by children and young people for a mental health concern in 2025.

That is up from 55,525 in 2019 with some of the biggest rises seen in very young children aged six to nine. The increases far outstrip the overall jump in attendances, which has risen by just over 8% over the period.

Doctors said the cases included children and young people brought in by families, carers and police – some of those in emotional crisis become aggressive or have challenging behaviour.

In total, more than 6,200, around 8%, waited over 12 hours in A&E.

RCPCH officer for mental health Dr Sam Jones said there was a lack of wider mental health care and, in particular, crisis support available in many parts of the country that meant these vulnerable children and young people were not getting the help they needed.

"Behind every one of these figures is a child or young person in distress and a family who didn't know where lese to turn.

"Emergency departments are a vital safety net, but they were never designed to be a place where children in mental health crisis wait for days at time.

"This is a national crisis that will only get worse without urgent intervention."

She said alongside greater investment in children's mental health services, staff from key agencies across health, social care and education needed better training in helping children who are struggling with their mental health.

Dr Mark Buchanan, of the Royal College of Emergency Medicine, said children and young people facing a mental health crisis were ending up in A&E by "default".

"They deserve care within systems and settings that are designed to meet their needs."

Gemma Byrne, of the mental health charity Mind, said: "A&E can be a frightening environment for anyone in mental health crisis, let alone a child. Making them spend more than 12 hours there is simply unacceptable.

She said children were not getting the support they need early enough.

"The current system, where many mental health services only provide support when young people are considered 'unwell enough' to qualify, clearly isn't working."

She said expanding the network of young future hubs, which bring together a range of support covering mental health, employment, sports and volunteering, was a crucial step.

The government is planning to publish a new mental health strategy later in the summer.

But a Department of Health and Social Care spokesman said improvements were already being made with investment in mental health teams for schools and more than 150 new mental health hubs in community locations such as banks and libraries .

"No child should have to reach crisis point before getting the support they need," he added.

Claire Evans, of Anna Freud, a mental health charity for children, young people and families, said the figures were deeply concerning.

"The new mental health strategy must place children at its heart, creating the conditions for lifelong positive mental health and accelerating investment in accessible, community-based support."

articles.title: Range Rover launches first fully electric model
articles.summary: The vehicle is being built at JLR's manufacturing plant in Solihull, in the West Midlands.
articles.body:
Range Rover has unveiled its first fully electric model, after a year‑long delay to its planned launch.

The Range Rover Electric, to be built in Solihull, marks a major shift in its electrification programme, backed by large‑scale upgrades across its West Midlands sites.

Parent company JLR said it had up-skilled 10,500 workers for electric production as it pushes ahead with modernisation despite recent financial pressures and planned job cuts.

The launch comes as the Coventry‑based carmaker faces falling profits, supply chain disruption and restructuring following a cyber attack last year.

The company said the launch was being supported by new battery and electric drive unit production lines as well as training around 9,000 employees in Solihull for electrification and a further 1,500 trained across the region.

JLR's Electric Propulsion Manufacturing Centre in Wolverhampton is now producing battery packs and electric drive units alongside internal combustion engines.

Martin Limpert, managing director of Range Rover, called the new model the result of a decade of "considered engineering".

JLR's electric roll-out comes after a turbulent year with profits dropping to £66m in the first quarter after a fire at a key Norwegian supplier.

The business is also undergoing restructuring, confirming that fewer than 300 roles will go less than a year after a cyber attack halted production for more than a month.

At the time of the results, the firm said new product launches would leave "JLR in good shape whilst acknowledging the continuing geopolitical, inflationary and regulatory challenges the industry faces".

articles.title: Presidents Cup 2026: Breaking Down The International Team Roster
articles.summary: The 2026 Presidents Cup is right around the corner. Team International and Team USA will face off at Medinah Country […]
articles.body:
The 2026 Presidents Cup is right around the corner. Team International and Team USA will face off at Medinah Country Club Sept. 24-27.

The best players not from the U.S. and Europe will face off against the Red, White and Blue. As a result, it will set the stage for fierce competition in the American Midwest at the end of the month.

Six players were automatically selected based on their success in the Official World Golf Ranking. The team of 12 is rounded out by six picks from International Captain Geoff Ogilvy.

Medinah Country Club becomes the only club in the world to have hosted a U.S. Open, a PGA Championship, a Ryder Cup and a Presidents Cup.

Let's break down this year's international squad.

The first automatic qualifier, Si Woo Kim, finished the FedEx Cup season at No. 13 in the world rankings. He will lead this squad as the highest-ranked player. Two years ago, Kim was one of five players on the International squad with two points but not enough in the Americans' seven-point victory. He recorded a win with Byeong Hun An over Scottie Scheffler and Russell Henley to cap off a 5-0 sweep in Friday's foursomes. This season, Kim logged 11 top 10s, including six top 5s. That includes runner-up finishes at the Farmers Insurance Open, the CJ Cup, the Byron Nelson, and the FedEx St. Jude Championship. He also registered third-place finishes at the WM Phoenix Open and the RBC Heritage.

Hideki Matsuyama will be appearing in his seventh consecutive Presidents Cup. Outside of Corey Conners and Christian Bezuidenhout, he is the only player from the last International team on this year's squad to earn a point in Sunday singles. He scored two birdies in the final three holes to record a 1-up win over Scheffler. This season, Matsuyama posted six top 10s and three top 5s, including a third-place finish at the 3M Open and a runner-up finish at the WM Phoenix Open. Matsuyama's iron game was strong, ranking seventh in approaches from more than 200 yards. He also ranked 22nd in both strokes gained total and strokes gained approach.

The reigning Open Champion will be making his first Presidents Cup starts. At No. 25 in the World Golf Rankings and at 39 years old, he will be making a dream come true. Representing New Zealand, his roots run deep, as his father, Grant, was the main goalkeeper for the famous All Blacks. This season was a year for him to put himself on the map with his victory at Royal Birkdale. He is also one of six players to appear at the Tour Championship last week.

Two years ago, Tom Kim brought the energy to this International Team. He had one of the shots to remember with a moonshot hole-out just from off the green before falling with Si Woo Kim to Patrick Cantlay and Xander Schauffele in Saturday's Foursomes. He also went toe to toe with Scheffler on the first day. Kim had a bounce-back 2026 season where he finished 94 th in the 2025 FedEx Cup standings and fell to 108 th that fall. After posting just one top 10 in 2025, Kim responded with four top 10s and three top 5s. It was highlighted by winning the Scottish Open in July.

Min Woo Lee returns to the International Team after his debut two years ago. Selected by captain Mike Weir, Lee earned 0.5 points with a draw at Royal Montreal. Now as an automatic qualifier, he has been cooking. He logged two runner-up finishes at Pebble Beach and at the Scottish Open. Lee recorded a third place in Houston in March before recording the best finish from the International Team at the Tour Championship, placing fourth. Lee has the chance to play a pivotal role in his second Presidents Cup.

The sixth and final automatic qualifier for Team International is Adam Scott. Scott, 46, is competing in his 12 th Presidents Cup. Already representing the international squad for the most appearances in Presidents Cup history, he will be tied with Phil Mickelson for the most appearances. He enters this year's Presidents Cup with 54 total matches with a 20-28-6 record. Only Mickelson has appeared in more matches at 55, and that record is expected to be broken as early as the second day. In 2026, Scott logged three top 10s, including fourth-place finishes at the Genesis Invitational and the Cadillac Championship. He also tied for ninth at the Open Championship before registering three top 16 finishes in each FedEx Cup playoff event.

Presidents Cup Captain Pick No. 1: Corey Conners

This is Corey Conners third straight Presidents Cup. It is his second time being picked. Two years ago at Royal Montreal, Conners recorded two points with a win in foursomes and a 5-and-3 win in singles. This season, the Canadian logged seven top 25s and a top 10 at the Travelers Championship. He finished outside the top 50 in the FedEx Cup standings at 59 th . Conners ranked 19 th in driving accuracy, which could be a pivotal piece when it comes to team play in foursomes.

Presidents Cup Captain Pick No. 2: Nico Echavarria

Nico Echavarria is Ogilvy's second pick and will be a rookie on this International Team. Echavarria logged three top 10s, highlighted by winning the Cognizant Classic in March. He also placed sixth at the Charles Schwab and eighth at Pebble Beach. Throughout the season, he played his best on the greens, ranking 51 st in strokes gained putting. Representing Colombia, this was a goal over the last 24 months.

Presidents Cup Captain Pick No. 3: Nick Taylor

As Echavarria had motivation for this Presidents Cup, so did Nick Taylor. Taylor, the Canadian, was snubbed from playing two years ago in a home Presidents Cup at Royal Montreal. He made the 92-foot eagle putt in a playoff to win the RBC Canadian Open a few years ago. This season, Taylor made five top 25s, including a T9 at the Cadillac Championship. Like Echavarria, his strength is his putting. He ranked one spot behind Echavarria in strokes gained putting, while also ranking 22nd in putts per round and 37 th in one-putt percentage. Taylor also ranked 42nd in driving accuracy. So, if he can drive and putt at a high level, he can be a player to watch.

Presidents Cup Captain Pick No. 4: Sungjae Im

Sungjae Im has become a veteran in this International Team locker room alongside Matsuyama and Scott. This is Im's fourth Presidents Cup and first time being picked since his first appearance in 2019 when he went 3-1-1 in Australia. He has winning Presidents Cup records in both Four-balls (3-2-1) and Singles (2-1). That includes taking down Cameron Young in Sunday singles in 2022. Im had a successful 2026 season highlighted by three top 5s. He ranked 22 nd on the PGA Tour in strokes gained putting. Im also ranked fifth in one-putt percentage and seventh in putts per round. He did suffer a wrist injury early in the year but got better as the season progressed.

Presidents Cup Captain Pick No. 5: Ryo Hisatsune

The first rookie chosen by Ogilvy is Ryo Hisatsune. Hisatsune is the second player on the International Team roster, alongside Matsuyama. He posted five top 10s this season, including a runner-up finish at the Farmers Insurance Open. He ranked ninth in greens regulation percentage and 21 in total driving. As a result, he can be partnered alongside Im or Taylor to have some success in team play.

Presidents Cup Captain Pick No. 6: Christiaan Bezuidenhout

Like Im, Christiaan Bezuidenhout is starting to become one of the more experienced players for the International Team. This is his third Presidents Cup start. That experience includes going 3-1-1 and 2-0 in singles play. The South African posted six top 25 finishes, including a T8 at the Puerto Rican Open and a T6 at Myrtle Beach. His statistics played a big role in his selection. Bezuidenhout ranked ninth in par-4 scoring average, 14th in strokes gained putting, 26th in strokes gained approach, and 24th in strokes gained total. He is also seventh in sand save percentage and 10 th in scrambling, which could be useful when it comes to the Four-balls.

One of the biggest names left off Ogilvy's roster is Jason Day. He provides that veteran presence, as this would have been his sixth Presidents Cup. Day ranked 11th in the International Team standings and was the highest-rated player not selected. His record also includes going 3-1-1 in 2013. The Aussie opened the season with a runner-up finish at The American Express and tied for sixth at the Texas Children's Houston Open. However, he did not play as well as the season progressed, missing the cut or withdrawing in four of his final five starts. He also did not make the FedEx Cup Playoffs and finished 82 nd .

articles.title: More than 180 Jewish entertainers rally behind actor Mark Ruffalo in protest letter
articles.summary: More than 180 Jewish artists signed a letter defending actor Mark Ruffalo after Paramount accused him of antisemitic tropes over his merger opposition.
articles.body: More than 180 Jewish entertainers and artists signed a letter on Tuesday "proudly" voicing support for actor Mark Ruffalo after he was accused of antisemitism in his opposition to the proposed Warner Bros. Discovery-Paramount merger. "We are Jewish artists, writers, creative professionals, faith leaders and thinkers who have, in response to the outrageous smear campaign against our respected colleague Mark Ruffalo, a simple message to share with the world: Enough!" the letter read, according to Variety. "Enough with the false and dangerous weaponization of charges of antisemitism against those who are brave enough to point out the obvious: that the assault on the Palestinian people and the assault on our liberties at home are deeply interconnected, and there is nothing antisemitic about recognizing that fact." Ruffalo was previously accused of invoking "antisemitic tropes" by Paramount after the Marvel star shared a video from August of Safra Catz, an Oracle executive vice chair and Paramount board member, discussing technology Oracle used to assist Israel after the Oct. 7 Hamas terrorist attacks. JOHN CUSACK STANDS IN 'SOLIDARITY' WITH MARK RUFFALO AMID PARAMOUNT'S ANTISEMITISM ALLEGATION He linked Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, the father of Paramount CEO David Ellison, to financing behind the proposed acquisition and suggested the merger would be used to push "oppression." "These ‘really profoundly scary technologies’ will most likely be merged into one of the largest media conglomerates in the world and one day used on you," Ruffalo said. "Look how she revels in what we now have come to see as a genocide, which was built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle." The Jewish artists, who include Abbi Jacobson, Alex Winter, Gina Gershon, Ilana Glazer, James Schamus, Joel Coen, Larry Charles, Kate Berlant, Naomi Klein, Sarah Sherman, Jane Schoenbrun, Todd Haynes and Tony Kushner, denied this comment was antisemitic, claiming executives "themselves have explicitly linked to their support for the ongoing depredations being visited on the people of Palestine and their silencing of critics of those horrors." "The AI road to WarnerMount runs through Gaza, and Ellison has often let us know the Orwellian world he has in store for us as he consolidates control over what we watch and how we watch it, knowing that as we watch he and his corrupt cohort will always be watching us," the letter read. JEWISH EDUCATORS FACE RAMPANT ANTISEMITISM IN TEACHERS UNIONS, NEW REPORT FINDS The celebrities also argued that a majority of American Jews now believe that Israel committed war crimes against Gaza, with a significant portion believing Israel is guilty of genocide. They called for an end to "spurious charges of antisemitism" against people like Ruffalo. "Pointing out the crucial connections between what is happening in Gaza and what is happening in Hollywood is the exact opposite of antisemitism. It is, for us, the very essence of Jewish ethical duty," the letter read. Fox News Digital reached out to Ruffalo's representatives for comment. Ruffalo previously denied pushing antisemitism in a statement to Fox News Digital after Paramount's original condemnation. MS RACHEL CONFRONTED ON ACCUSING ISRAEL OF 'GENOCIDE' IN PARK INTERACTION WITH PODCASTER "The accusation that I am antisemitic is appalling and fundamentally dishonest," Ruffalo said. "Criticizing the actions of the Israeli prime minister, a military technology contract or the executives who supply it is not the same as criticizing Jewish people." Ruffalo continued to receive backlash after a group of nearly 1,000 industry insiders, calling itself The Brigade, released a statement condemning the actor last week. "This is not commentary on a merger. It is not a criticism of a government. It is simple antisemitism, where Jewish executives are portrayed as a secretive and powerful wealth-hoarding elite delighting in mass death," the statement read. Elizabeth Barcohana, the California Republican Party’s Jewish engagement chair, told Fox News Digital on Thursday that Ruffalo’s prominence in the opposition to the merger reflected Hollywood’s liberal political activism, while praising The Brigade for challenging him. "Ruffalo as an anti-merger spokesman is an odd choice given his extremist rhetoric that has completely discredited him with rational people," Barcohana said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP She added, "He is an activist more than an actor (indeed maybe that’s one in the same). I applaud The Brigade for organizing an oppositional force against the explosion of antisemitism within Hollywood and standing up to Ruffalo’s Israel Derangement Syndrome."

articles.body: A new post circulating on X has put Candace Owens’ latest comments about Turning Point USA back under the spotlight. In the clip shown in the screenshot, Owens questions the direction of the organization while suggesting that another group could eventually take its place. articles.body: This article was originally published on CFR.org and updated by NBC News. The Trump administration announced in January 2026 that it was indefinitely freezing visa processing for nationals of 75 countries, one in a series of immigration restrictions rolled out since President Donald Trump’s return to office. State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said the visa pause was aimed at people who were likely to be a “public charge”—a term for someone reliant on public benefits for basic needs. A federal court struck down the visa pause in August. That same month, the administration temporarily paused the processing of immigrant visa appointments worldwide for consular officer training, though the pause is not expected to last beyond early to-mid-September.
